text: Gender-affirming surgery (GAS) is a surgical procedure or series of procedures that alter a person's physical appearance and sexual characteristics to align with their gender identity. It is most commonly associated with transgender health care but is also pursued by cisgender individuals. The term is also known as sex reassignment surgery (SRS), gender confirmation surgery (GCS), and other names; however, "sex change" is generally considered offensive. Feminizing surgeries, such as vaginoplasty, vulvoplasty, and breast augmentation, result in female-looking anatomy, while masculinizing surgeries, including phalloplasty, mastectomy, and hysterectomy, result in male-looking anatomy. Patients often require lifelong hormone replacement therapy to support their endocrine system. Professional medical organizations, such as the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH), have established Standards of Care that require psychological evaluation and a period of real-life experience living in the desired gender before surgery is considered. Sweden became the first country to allow transgender people to change their legal gender after reassignment surgery and provide free hormone treatment in 1972, followed by Singapore in 1973 as the first in Asia. GAS is sometimes referred to as bottom surgery (in contrast to top surgery on the chest), and WPATH defines it broadly to include any surgical procedure for gender dysphoria. For trans women, genital reconstruction typically involves vaginoplasty using techniques like penile inversion, rectosigmoid vaginoplasty, or peritoneal pullthrough vaginoplasty; a less invasive option is vulvoplasty, which creates external female genitalia without a vaginal canal. For trans men, procedures may include phalloplasty or metoidioplasty to construct a penis, with metoidioplasty using the clitoris and resulting in a sensation-perceiving penis head, and scrotoplasty with possible testicular implants. Bigenital operations, such as androgynoplasty or vagina-preserving phalloplasty, allow individuals to retain original organs and are rarely performed. Gender nullification, which removes all external genitalia except the urethral opening, is pursued by some individuals assigned male at birth. GAS is also pursued by cisgender people for procedures like mammaplasty, penile implants, or testicular implants after orchiectomy. The term is often misrepresented by anti-trans activists as "genital-mutilation surgery." WPATH lists medically necessary procedures as including complete hysterectomy, bilateral mastectomy, chest reconstruction or augmentation, genital reconstruction, and certain facial plastic reconstructions, as well as facial hair electrolysis. Historical cases include Roman Emperor Elagabalus (2nd century), Alan L. Hart (1917), Dora Richter (1922–1931), and Lili Elbe (1930–1931), who underwent multiple surgeries including orchiectomy, penectomy, vaginoplasty, and an experimental uterine transplant that was rejected. In 1951, Harold Gillies developed a phalloplasty technique that became a standard. In 1971, Roberto Farina performed Brazil’s first male-to-female surgery, and in 1984, Jalma Jurado developed a technique used in over 500 surgeries. In 1999, Lebovic and Laub developed metoidioplasty. In 2003, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in favor of Carola van Kück, affirming access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy. In 2011, Christiane Völling won a landmark case against a surgeon for non-consensual sex reassignment. As of 2017, some European countries require forced sterilization for legal gender recognition, and Japan requires sterilization as of 2020. The prevalence of transgender-related surgeries is difficult to measure, with a 2015 U.S. survey reporting that 25% of respondents had undergone such surgery. Medical conditions like diabetes, asthma, and HIV can complicate treatment, and patients typically require a multidisciplinary healthcare team, including endocrinologists and pharmacists, for medication management and education. Fertility is a key consideration, as orchiectomy or oophorectomy results in irreversible infertility. Surgery is generally not performed on children under 18, though rare exceptions exist with long-term mental health counseling and parental or court consent. Infants with intersex conditions may undergo early interventions, which are controversial due to human rights concerns. Negative outcomes, including PTSD and suicide, can occur when the surgically assigned gender does not match gender identity. Milton Diamond recommended delaying surgery until children can give informed consent and suggested introducing them to others with differences of sex development to reduce stigma. Access to GAS is limited by financial barriers, insurance coverage, and provider availability, with many surgeons trained under Standards of Care, particularly WPATH’s, which are widely recognized but criticized for being rigid and restrictive. Many surgeons require two letters of recommendation, one from a mental health professional with over a year of experience diagnosing gender dysphoria, confirming surgery is appropriate. While many medical professionals oppose requiring surgery for legal gender change, many jurisdictions still require a physician’s letter attesting to surgery for legal recognition. In the U.S., an increasing number of insurance plans cover GAS, including genital reconstruction, chest reconstruction, breast augmentation, and hysterectomy, with some requiring proof of psychological evaluation and real-life experience (RLE). In June 2008, the American Medical Association stated that denying treatment for gender dysphoria constitutes discrimination and supports insurance coverage as recommended by physicians. In 2017, the U.S. Defense Health Agency approved payment for sex reassignment surgery for an active-duty trans woman, performed at a private hospital due to lack of expertise in military facilities. Long-term quality-of-life research is limited by small sample sizes and baseline mental health disparities. A 2020 meta-analysis found low-quality evidence that chest reconstruction improves quality of life; a 2022 review found reduced suicide attempts, anxiety, depression, and gender dysphoria, along with higher life satisfaction; a 2024 review found genital surgeries improved depression and dissociation, with mixed results for other mental health outcomes and less conclusive evidence of improvement compared to hormonal therapy. A secondary analysis of the U.S. Transgender Survey found that gender-affirming surgery was significantly associated with lower rates of psychological distress, smoking, and suicidal ideation among those who underwent it compared to those who desired but did not undergo surgery.

A 2020 meta-analysis found "evidence of low quality" that gender-affirming surgery, especially chest reconstruction for trans men, improves quality of life.[71] A 2022 systematic review indicated that gender-affirming surgical procedures were linked to reduced rates of suicide attempts, anxiety, depression, and gender dysphoria, along with higher levels of life satisfaction, happiness, and quality of life after surgery.[72] A 2024 systematic review found that genital surgeries significantly improved depression and dissociation in trans and gender-diverse individuals, with "mixed results" for other mental health outcomes, concluding there was "less conclusive evidence" of mental health improvement after trans surgical procedures compared to hormonal therapy, though expressing tentative support for both.[70] A secondary analysis of the U.S. Transgender Survey found that gender-affirming surgery was significantly associated with lower rates of psychological distress, smoking, and suicidal ideation compared to those who desired surgery but had not undergone it; this was the largest controlled study on the subject to date (N=19,960), though limitations due to survey design and self-reported responses introduced possible response bias.[73] Gender-affirming surgery can be viewed as human enhancement.[74] Transgender people often face social obstacles such as discrimination, prejudice, harassment, and stigmatizing behaviors, with rejection being more severe than for lesbians, gays, and bisexuals,[72][75] which may limit quality of life improvements from surgery and prevent full alleviation of mental health disparities post-procedure.[77] Regret after gender-affirming surgery may stem from poor social and group support, late-onset gender transition, poor sexual functioning, and mental health problems; however, a 2021 systematic review found regret to be low, at around 1% among 7.928 transgender patients studied.[78] Regarding genital sensitivity, both trans men and trans women can maintain sensitivity after surgery, depending on surgical techniques used to preserve it; preserving the clitoral hood and clitoris under the reconstructed phallus is critical for maintaining sensitivity and achieving orgasm after phalloplasty.[79][80] Erogenous sensitivity is measured by the ability to reach orgasm during masturbation or intercourse; studies show both trans men and trans women report increased orgasms in sexual activities,[81][82] indicating the potential to maintain or enhance genital sensitivity. Most trans individuals report improved sex lives and greater sexual satisfaction after surgery,[82] with this enhancement positively linked to satisfaction with new primary sex characteristics.[82] Before surgery, trans patients had unwanted sex organs they wished to remove, leading to lack of enthusiasm for sexual activity; after surgery, they report greater body satisfaction and less stress during sexual activity.[82] Most report experiencing sexual excitement during sexual activity and masturbation,[82] with orgasm frequency and intensity differing between trans men and trans women—almost all female-to-male individuals report increased sexual excitement and can achieve orgasm through partnered sex or masturbation,[82][81] while only 85% of male-to-female individuals achieve orgasm after surgery.[83] Both groups report qualitative changes in orgasm experiences: female-to-male individuals report intensified and stronger excitement and orgasms, while male-to-female individuals report longer, gentler experiences.[82] Masturbation frequency increases after surgery for both trans women and trans men; a study found 78% of transsexuals can achieve orgasm through masturbation post-surgery,[81][82][84] with female-to-male individuals masturbating more frequently than male-to-female, possibly due to increased libido from testosterone therapy or reduced gender dysphoria.[81] Among life aspects, sexual satisfaction is the lowest among physical, emotional, and social domains; when compared to cisgender peers, trans women have similar sexual satisfaction to cis women, but trans men have lower satisfaction than cis men, and trans men also report lower sexual satisfaction than trans women.[81]
